title: Apply accurate information about HIV & AIDS to everyday life

lessons.title: What HIV and AIDS are and how HIV spreads
lessons.html:
What HIV and AIDS are

HIV is a virus. It attacks the body's defence system. This defence system is called the immune system. It fights germs and keeps you well.

When HIV is not treated, it slowly damages the immune system. After some years the body cannot fight other illnesses well. Then a person can get sick with TB, pneumonia, thrush and other infections. This late stage is called AIDS.

A person can have HIV and look and feel healthy for many years. You cannot see HIV by looking at someone. The only way to know is to test.

How HIV spreads

HIV lives in some body fluids. It spreads when these fluids from a person with HIV get into another person's body:

  • Blood
  • Semen and fluid from the vagina during sex without a condom
  • From a mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding, if she is not on treatment
  • Sharing needles or blades that have blood on them

How HIV does NOT spread

You do not get HIV from everyday work and living together. HIV does not spread by:

  • Shaking hands, hugging or working side by side in the stable yard
  • Sharing cups, plates, food or a toilet
  • Mosquito bites or other insect bites
  • Touching horses or other animals
  • Sweat, tears or coughing

Blood at work

On a farm or in a stable yard people get cuts from wire, tools or tack. When a worker is bleeding, help them, but protect yourself:

  1. Put on gloves from the first aid box before you touch blood.
  2. If there are no gloves, use a clean plastic bag over your hand.
  3. Let the injured person press on their own wound with a cloth if they can.
  4. Wash your hands with soap and water afterwards.
  5. Report the injury to your supervisor.

Never touch another person's blood with bare hands if you can avoid it. This rule protects everyone, whatever their HIV status. First aid needs hands-on training from an accredited provider.

lessons.title: Protecting yourself and living positively
lessons.html:
Ways to protect yourself

You can lower your risk of HIV with a few simple steps:

  • Use a condom every time you have sex. Condoms are free at clinics and many workplaces.
  • Have fewer sexual partners and talk openly with your partner.
  • Never share razor blades, needles or tattoo tools.
  • Get tested, and ask your partner to test too.
  • Go to the clinic quickly if you have signs of a sexual infection. These infections make HIV easier to catch.

Testing

An HIV test is quick. Clinics test for free. The result is private. Only you decide who to tell. Knowing your status early is good, because treatment can start early.

Treatment works

There is no cure for HIV yet. But there is very good treatment. The medicine is called ARVs (antiretrovirals). ARVs are free at government clinics.

  • Take ARVs every day, at the same time, as the clinic tells you.
  • Do not stop when you feel better.
  • Go back to the clinic for check-ups and blood tests.

A person on ARVs can live a long, healthy life and keep working. When the treatment keeps the virus very low, the person does not pass HIV to a partner through sex. A mother on treatment can protect her baby.

Living positively

Eat good food, sleep enough, do not drink too much alcohol and do not smoke. Treat TB and other illnesses quickly.

Respect at work

Workers with HIV have the same rights as other workers. In South Africa the Employment Equity Act says it is unfair to discriminate against a worker because of HIV status. A worker does not have to tell the employer their status. Do not gossip, make jokes or refuse to work with someone. Stigma stops people from testing and getting help.

Example: Sipho on a stud farm tells his friend he is on ARVs. His friend keeps the secret and still shares lunch with him. That is the right way.

Key points

  • HIV spreads through blood, sex without a condom, and mother to baby.
  • It does not spread through hugging, sharing cups or working together.
  • Use gloves when you help someone who is bleeding.
  • Testing is free and private; ARVs are free and must be taken every day.
  • Treat workers with HIV with respect; discrimination is against the law.
